title: Three-pillar framework for currency analysis
claim: Effective currency analysis integrates fundamental (PPP, REER, regression models), positioning (CFTC, risk reversals), and technical (trends, oscillators, patterns) perspectives rather than relying on a single methodology.
support: Framework diagram (Figure I.1) and multi-chapter development across all parts of the book.
mechanism: Different analytical lenses reveal valuations and price action at different time horizons and market regimes.
assumptions: Time horizon matters (long-run vs. medium vs. short-term)
failure_modes: Single-pillar approach misses regime transitions
Over-weighting one pillar leads to costly surprises

title: Purchasing Power Parity as long-run currency anchor
claim: PPP theory posits that exchange rates should adjust such that equivalent baskets of goods cost the same in different countries over the long run. PPP is best applied to multi-year time horizons and is less useful for tactical or short-term decisions.
support: Economic theory; historical examples (Mexico 1994, etc.); acknowledged limitations in real markets.
mechanism: Inflation differentials drive long-run exchange-rate adjustment; persistent deviations are unsustainable.
assumptions: Goods mobility and price arbitrage work over long horizons
Non-tradeables and capital flows are secondary
failure_modes: PPP deviations persist for years (as shown in 1990s-2000s dollar strength)
Real shocks (productivity, terms of trade) move equilibrium
Capital flows dominate in medium term

title: Internal-external balance model for exchange-rate equilibrium
claim: Long-run equilibrium real exchange rate reflects internal balance (full employment) and external balance (sustainable current account). Unsustainable current-account deficits force currency depreciation.

source.section: Real Exchange Rates and the External Balance

support: Economic equilibrium theory; specific examples: US productivity boom 1995-1999 accompanied strong dollar; Mexico 1994 crisis forced peso devaluation.
mechanism: Expansionary fiscal policy creates current-account deficits; exchange-rate depreciation restores balance by reducing import demand and raising export competitiveness.
failure_modes: Deficits can persist longer than theory predicts (e.g., US 1980s-2000s)
Capital inflows can finance deficits indefinitely

title: Three-horizon fair-value regression framework
claim: Currency fair value can be estimated using three regression models: (1) monthly using macro/financial data over 15+ years, (2) weekly over 52 weeks, (3) daily over 60 days. Coefficients change over time; no single model works across regimes.
support: EUR/USD monthly regression (1993-2009) with inflation ratio, bond spreads, S&P 500: F-stat 16.7, R-squared 0.25, std error 0.14. Rolling 36-month correlations show variables change sign repeatedly.
mechanism: Shorter windows adapt to changing market relationships; longer windows capture structural factors. Confidence bands tighten as horizon shortens.
failure_modes: 2008 EUR/USD spike exceeded 6 standard deviations from model
Iraq invasion caused dummy variable t-stat 11.6 structural shift
Rolling correlations show variables flip sign periodically

title: CFTC non-commercial positioning as trend-exhaustion signal
claim: Extremes in CFTC non-commercial (speculative) futures positions correlate with price-trend peaks/troughs; peaks suggest speculators have exhausted capacity to drive trends and may reverse.
support: EUR/USD 2000-2008: net long position vs. price shows weak 0.27 correlation; deviation from 26wma shows improved alignment of peaks/troughs.
mechanism: Net positioning reflects aggregate speculator sentiment; extreme net longs/shorts indicate crowded trades vulnerable to reversal when catalysts emerge.
failure_modes: CFTC data released Friday afternoon (late, low liquidity)
Data is 3 days old by release
Open interest more than doubled 2000-2008; same positioning size means different things
2006-2008 EUR/USD rally saw positioning rise then drop while price kept rising

title: Options risk-reversal skew as real-time sentiment indicator
claim: Risk-reversal premium (difference in implied volatility of puts vs. calls) reveals options-market participants' directional bias. Extreme risk-reversal levels suggest off-balance positioning and potential for sharp reversals; data is real-time (not delayed like CFTC).
support: Risk reversals are publicly quoted; provide intra-day updates vs. CFTC's Friday release.
mechanism: Options traders' skew reflects fear/greed asymmetry; extreme skew indicates consensus view is vulnerable.
assumptions: Options market reflects true marginal sentiment
Skew data is observable and actionable
failure_modes: Risk reversals provide entry/exit hints but ambiguous stop/target levels
Can be in overbought/oversold state for extended periods

title: Moving averages reveal trend onset and persistence
claim: Moving averages (13wma, 26wma, 52wma) smooth price action; crossovers of price or shorter-term MA through longer-term MA indicate trend initiation. Lag and false signals occur in trendless markets; trend persistence often offsets whipsaw losses.
support: USD/JPY 1999-2008 shows clear trends totaling 121 pips over decade.
mechanism: Trend-follower logic: at trend onset, price separates from MA; moving averages lag but capture directional bias. In choppy markets, whipsaws accumulate.
assumptions: Lag is acceptable for risk management
failure_modes: Sharp pullbacks trigger false exit signals (MA lag)
Choppy markets produce whipsaws
MA lag means signal lags price move onset

title: RSI oscillator as overbought/oversold signal
claim: Relative Strength Index (RSI, typically 14-period) measures strength of upward vs. downward moves; RSI > 70 signals overbought (potential reversal), RSI < 30 signals oversold (potential bounce). Extreme levels in strong trends cause prolonged whipsaws.
support: EUR/USD 1998-2008 backtest: RSI signals generated 48.9% win rate, 3.8% avg gain vs. 2.6% avg loss, but 28.9% cumulative profit with 20%+ drawdown periods.
mechanism: RSI extremes reflect exhaustion of trend direction; reversals often follow, but strong trends can sustain extreme RSI levels for weeks/months.
failure_modes: Strong uptrends keep RSI > 70 for months, causing false exit signals
Strong downtrends keep RSI < 30 for months
Whipsaws on pullbacks within trends destroy profitability

title: Slow stochastics capture major trend reversals but generate many false signals
claim: Slow stochastic (5 fast, 3 slow smoothing) identifies overbought/oversold states; signals at 50 level crossover. Captures major reversals (e.g., GBP/USD 1999, 2001, 2004, 2005, 2007) but only 39-46% win rate on all signals.
support: GBP/USD 1999-2008: 67 total signals, 26 profitable (39%), avg win 1.3%, avg loss 1.01%; AUD/USD 1999-2008: 67 signals, 31 profitable (46%), avg win 3.8%, avg loss 2.6%, 26.6% cumulative profit but 23% drawdown.
mechanism: Stochastic extremes align with sentiment shifts; crossovers mid-range are noise.
assumptions: Extreme-level crossovers are more predictive than mid-range
failure_modes: High false-signal rate (61% GBP/USD, 54% AUD/USD)
Cumulative drawdowns 20-30%
Currency/period dependent

title: No single technical indicator works consistently across time and currencies
claim: Book case studies (EUR/USD RSI, GBP/USD stochastic, AUD/USD stochastic) show dramatically different profitability (28.9% EUR/USD, -16.2% GBP/USD, +26.6% AUD/USD) and win rates (48.9%, 39%, 46%) on the same signal logic. Implication: technical signals require per-currency and per-regime calibration or ensemble approaches.
support: Three parallel case studies (EUR/USD RSI, GBP/USD stochastic, AUD/USD stochastic) in Ch8 with identical logic applied to different pairs.
mechanism: Different currencies have different trend persistence, volatility regimes, and carry characteristics. Indicator parameters optimal for one pair fail for another.
assumptions: Indicators are defined identically across pairs
failure_modes: Over-fitting to one pair; poor out-of-sample performance on others
Parameter sensitivity requires constant recalibration

title: Technical patterns as psychological turning points
claim: Chart patterns (head-and-shoulders, key-day reversals, support/resistance levels, Fibonacci retracements) reflect crowd psychology at key turning points. Patterns work until they do not; they identify levels where traders collectively respond.
support: Framework presentation; historical price charts with pattern overlays; pragmatic stance (patterns important if traders believe them important).
mechanism: Self-fulfilling: if enough participants recognize a pattern and trade at expected levels, the pattern becomes predictive.
assumptions: Crowd psychology is collective enough to move markets
failure_modes: Patterns work until they do not: price breaks pattern neckline without bouncing
Subjectivity in pattern identification
Pattern failure can be violent

title: Combined fundamental-positioning-technical framework produces actionable signals
claim: Case studies demonstrate that integrating all three pillars (fundamental fair-value deviation, CFTC positioning extremes, technical indicator signals) reduces false signals and improves win rate vs. single-pillar approaches.
support: Worked examples combining regression fair value with positioning and technical analysis; specific entry/exit levels and risk levels given.
mechanism: Filters: (1) Fundamental says currency is cheap/dear, (2) Positioning shows extremes, (3) Technical provides entry trigger. Reduces whipsaws.
assumptions: Filtering reduces noise more than it reduces signal
failure_modes: Too many filters → missed opportunities
Correlated signals in crisis regimes

title: Oscillator drawdowns highlight regime-change risk
claim: Book case studies show 20-30% drawdowns in oscillator strategies during persistent trends (EUR/USD 2006-2008, AUD/USD 2007). Implication: regime-detection filters (e.g., trend strength, volatility regime) are essential to avoid prolonged whipsaw periods.
support: EUR/USD RSI case: 20%+ drawdowns Apr 1999-Jun 2000, Jun 2006-Jun 2008 (both strong trend regimes). Stochastic cases: GBP/USD -25.5%, AUD/USD -23%.
mechanism: Oscillators assume mean reversion; strong trends violate assumption. Whipsaws accumulate when assumption breaks.
assumptions: Regimes can be detected in real-time
failure_modes: Regime detection is lagged
Regime transitions are ambiguous
Filter reduces signal but not whipsaws

title: CFTC positioning data lag and timing risk
claim: CFTC non-commercial positioning data are released late Friday afternoon (low liquidity in US market), are 3 days old, and may reflect positions already unwinding or corrected by release. Relying on CFTC data for intra-week or Monday trading is risky.
support: Book explicitly acknowledges: data are "three days old by the time they are published" and released "late on Friday afternoon in the United States—hardly the best of times for liquidity."
mechanism: Friday afternoon release coincides with low USD market liquidity and elevated weekend FX volatility risk.
assumptions: Market participants monitor Friday CFTC release
failure_modes: Position corrections already underway by Friday close
Weekend gap risk
Low liquidity Friday = poor execution on CFTC-driven trades
